An immutable type has to be rebuildable from what it hands back. `GradientOptions` first exposed spans but accepted arrays, reading "no stops" as an empty span and writing it as `null`, so recolouring a gradient cost a `ToArray()` and a ternary, and leaving out the ternary silently dropped the stops. The constructor now takes spans, empty meaning evenly distributed on both sides, and the round trip is one expression. In general, a value type whose getter and constructor disagree about representation shows up in the migration guide as an unreadable line, the wrong place to fix it.

Equality is now written by hand over the elements and the array is private, which also makes the record's shallow copy safe: `Default with { Direction = … }` shares the colours with `Default`, and neither instance hands the array out. The documented guarantee is "immutable through the API", not "immutable", because `MemoryMarshal` and reflection can get past it. Callers need not see that caveat, but the qualifier stops a later change from treating the array as unreachable. Dropping the record was tried first and rejected: it took `with` away while the three generator options kept it, and the defect was the public array, not the record. `IconData`, demoted the same way in the same change, was restored for the same reason.

Styling reaches the data modules, never the finder patterns. `WithModuleShape(shape, sizePercent)` and its renderer parameters style the data. The finders are drawn as one continuous concentric pattern whatever is asked for, and only `WithFinderPatternShape` (on all three builders) changes them. This follows from how each is read. A data module is sampled at its cell centre, so gaps around it cost nothing. A finder is located by its 1:1:3:1:1 run of dark and light, which a gap of one fiftieth of a module destroys: the dark three-module centre becomes three runs, and the ratio is nowhere in the image. At 98 % module size, on every symbology, neither this library nor ZXing found the symbol, so the old behaviour produced a non-conformant symbol, not a styled one. ISO/IEC 15415 grades fixed-pattern damage separately from data for the same reason.

Alignment patterns need no such protection and get none: they are found from a predicted position by their single dark centre module, and still decode at version 40 when shrunk to 75 %. The full-size square path stays in the merged-run renderer, where the finder is already solid, so the fast path is untouched. Only the per-module path changes, and gets cheaper: three rectangles per finder instead of thirty-three module draws.

Modules stay square at every canvas aspect ratio the builder accepts, so `WithSize(w, h)` fits rather than stretches. This invariant is narrower than "every canvas produces a readable symbol": a reader also needs enough pixels per module, on which `WithSize` has no lower bound, and a canvas can starve the short side without being small (4000x30 is 0.91 px/module and nothing reads it), so the fit removes one failure mode, not all. The symbol is drawn at one uniform module scale, centered, and leftover canvas is padded with `clearColor` when set, else the background colour. Both halves correct the same defect on the square symbologies. rMQR was built this way, except that its pad on an explicit canvas was transparent.

The stretch dated back to the 2019 renderer, which divided the area by columns and rows independently, and to a public API that took width and height separately from its first release. Never chosen or tested, it survived into 2.0.0 behind a `preserveAspectRatio` flag whose comment said only that the square symbologies "keep the historical fill behavior". The defect was undetectable rather than merely ugly: module centres stayed correct, so the data was intact and no call threw, but rectangular cells keep the finder's 1:1:3:1:1 run on one axis only.

A sweep of several payloads, four stylings and both orientations through this library and ZXing.Net showed failures from about 1.25:1 and no read by either decoder past about 1.8:1. In between, the outcome depends on the payload, the styling and the squeezed axis. The decoders disagree by direction: on wide renders this library reads many that ZXing does not, and on tall ones the reverse, though that half depends on running ZXing with AutoRotate. No threshold is worth quoting. `WithSize(900, 450)` silently returned an image neither reads. Outside that sweep, zxing-cpp reads the migration guide's example, though not every payload.

The pad default follows from the same rule, that a default must not silently return a defective image. Transparent is the wrong default: it becomes black bands once the image is encoded as JPEG and costs the opaque-surface optimization, and naming `clearColor` still gives transparent surroundings around an opaque symbol. The pad is painted around the content, not under it, so a translucent background is not blended twice.

The low-level renderer fits its area too, so the library has one geometry rule (2026-09-11): `SymbolRenderer.Render(canvas, area, …)` and the `SKCanvas.Render` extensions draw Standard QR and Micro QR at one uniform module scale, centered in the area, with the background over the whole area, as rMQR's overload always did. The public `GetFinderPatternRect` and `GetIconRects` fit the same way, because they answer for the area the caller passed to `Render` and would otherwise point beside what was drawn.

For a day after the builders stopped stretching, the renderer kept the fill as the only remaining way to pre-distort a symbol for an output device whose dots are not square. The plan was to give the builders an axis-aware module size before making the renderer fit, but its premise was false: pre-distortion never needed a stretched area. A non-uniform canvas scale over a square area gives exactly the old fill's pixels for plain modules and solid-colour finders (0 differing pixels across four aspect ratios). Styled output (shaped modules or finders, gradients and icons) is drawn in the square and stretched with it, which can differ from the old fill. A square area passes through the fit unchanged. So the renderer fits, and the device case goes through the canvas transform, where a caller who owns the canvas already expresses such things.

The builder-level `WithModulePixelSize(x, y)` waits for a concrete request: the device use case was named in review to justify the fill, with no report behind it. It would also have to be a transform over square cells, since the renderer fits any non-square area it is handed to a square, and a path that skipped the fit would get styled modules wrong: `CircleModuleShape` sizes its dot from the cell's shorter side and would print squashed, and the rounded shapes take their corner radius from that side and would print uneven corners.

The fit is taken from the shorter side, not through a module scale. An area square to within float rounding comes back exactly as given, so a square area draws as before and fitting twice equals fitting once, which the renderer relies on when it hands an already-fitted area to the helpers. The rounding slack is required: `SKRect.Create(x, y, s, s)` stores right and bottom as rounded sums, so a square at fractional coordinates is often a float step from square, and shrinking it by that step moved module edges by a pixel. Two float steps per axis is the floor, not a margin: a square whose four edges are each scaled, as a canvas scale produces, comes back two steps from square (measured over three million built with `SKRect.Create`, centre-and-half and `SKMatrix.MapRect`).

The cost of that floor is that far from the origin, where a step is a large share of the area, a non-square rectangle passes as square: at 1e9 a step is 64, so a 400x600 area is stored as 384x576, one and a half steps from square, and drawn square. Nothing renders correctly there anyway, since the same step quantises every module edge, and no slack can tell the two cases apart, because the rectangle is closer to square, in steps, than a real scaled square. Measured on a 400 px symbol, the two limits are far apart: a square area stops decoding at a coordinate of 1.68e7 (2^24), where a step reaches 2 and the module edges quantise, while the slack accepts a 1.5:1 area only from 4.38e8 (2^28.7), twenty-six times further out. Inside the range that still decodes, the slack accepts a stretch of about 1 % at most (1.011:1 at a coordinate of 1e7), against the 1.25:1 where reading starts to fail, so it cannot cost a read. The precision is lost in the caller's `SKRect` before the renderer sees it, so no signature taking one can recover it. A caller working at such coordinates keeps the area near the origin and places it with the canvas transform, which the rasteriser prefers anyway.

All three symbologies refuse an inverted (negative width or height) or non-finite area with `ArgumentException`. An inverted rect can mean a mirror or the same bounds written backwards, different pictures for an asymmetric symbol, so neither is guessed. A mirrored symbol is requested with a canvas scale of -1 about the area, as with pre-distortion. The decoder reads mirrored captures, so strict output and tolerant input stay the pair.

A zero-size area draws nothing rather than throwing, because a canvas before layout or a collapsed panel routinely produces one. The check is on the fitted symbol, so anything sized in pixels rather than cells (an icon border, a caption, a caller-written shape) stops there too, but invalid icon settings are still refused, since a collapsed panel must not hide a mistake until it opens. An area whose fitted symbol has no size keeps its background, since the area is the caller's and only the symbol is missing. An aspect ratio past about 2^25 reaches that state without being zero, because centring puts the symbol's offset where its shorter side rounds away (rMQR's rectangle survives about three powers of two longer than the square symbologies').

The canvas extensions check every argument, the gradient direction included, before they clear the canvas, so a refused call leaves the canvas as it was. Rounding still differs from the builders: the builders floor the centering offset to whole pixels because they own the canvas, and the renderer uses the fit as computed because its area may sit under the caller's transform, so an odd leftover can shift edges by half a pixel.

The decoder keeps its tolerance for non-square modules, because symbols arrive from thermal printers, laser markers and perspective: the encoder never produces non-square modules, and the decoder accepts them. The tolerance's measured edge is the same for all three symbologies and both directions (plain modules 8 px on the short side, three payloads of different versions per symbology, every right-angle rotation, 2026-09-27): every render decodes up to 2.35:1, at 2.40:1 only the largest Standard QR payload does, and from 2.45:1 none do. The edge comes from the finder cross-check, which allows a column at most 12/5 of its row's length, a window sized for keystoned finders. Widened to 4, the same renders decode to 3.5:1. Before that window (2026-09-26) the column had to be within 40 % of the row, and the edge measured on 2026-09-12 was about 1.38:1.

With the builders and the renderer fitting every area, only a canvas scale makes such a symbol, so the decoder tests draw theirs that way and measure the finder's centre stone on both axes to prove the stretch is in the pixels. The tests they replaced had drawn square modules unnoticed ever since the canvas fit.

A public class with no designed extension point is sealed: the three data types, the three image builders, `IconData` and `GradientOptions`. The extension points are the shape hierarchies (`ModuleShape`, `FinderPatternShape`, `IconShape`) and `SymbolImageBuilderBase<TSelf>`, whose `private protected` constructor keeps derivation inside the rendering package.

## Why

### Why three packages under a new name

Issue #370 named the 1.x library's two strengths, SkiaSharp integration and speed with low memory, and their conflict: anyone who wanted only the QR module matrices still paid for SkiaSharp. The cost was never the managed assembly (95 KB trimmed to QR encode only) but `libSkiaSharp`: 11.9 MB per RID, untrimmable, deployed whether or not a Skia call survives, and the part that needs CVE tracking. Only a package boundary changes a dependency graph, so the 2.0.0 major version split the package into a dependency-free core and a rendering package (the core split, 2026-09-04 to 2026-09-06).

The core is not `SkiaSharp.QrCode.Core`: a dependency-free package must not carry the name of the dependency it is free of, which would mislead the audience the split is for and stops making sense at the second non-Skia renderer (`SkiaSharp.QrCode.ImageSharp` is nonsense). The `SkiaSharp.*` prefix is reserved on nuget.org but public, so the ID could have been pushed. It was rejected on meaning, not mechanics. The brand became `FeatherQR`: "Feather" is the established .NET word for lightweight (`FeatherHttp`, `Feather.Blazor`, `DotFeather`), lightweight is the issue's title, and the compound name was free on nuget.org, npm, crates.io, PyPI and GitHub. Every speed word considered was a benchmark claim, a live product, a reduced-feature connotation, a language, a fictional symbology next to Micro QR, or a .NET-only term. "Package architecture" defines what the name may mean, so it never has to be defended against a byte count.

`SkiaSharp.QrCode` survives as an empty metapackage because NuGet has no redirect: of its three mechanisms (keeping an ID, deprecating it with an alternate, one-way and for retiring, and a metapackage), only a metapackage keeps an existing `<PackageReference Include="SkiaSharp.QrCode" />` restoring after the upgrade, which matters with four million downloads behind it. New documentation leads with `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp`. The metapackage is for compatibility only and stays as long as 1.x packages are listed.

Each package has one namespace, `FeatherQR` and `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp`, and nothing is type-forwarded. The former `SkiaSharp.QrCode.Image` sub-namespace is merged into the rendering namespace, because the major version changes every `using` line anyway. The same major version renames types, so a forward would preserve nothing anyone can compile against.

`TryDecode(SKBitmap)` is a C# 14 extension member with a named fallback. A static method cannot be added to a type from another assembly, every renderer package has the same need, and extension blocks solve it once: `QRCodeImageDecoder` (and its Micro QR and rMQR twins) declares `extension(QRCodeDecoder)` with the bitmap overloads, which the compiler emits as ordinary public static methods on the enclosing class. So a C# 14 consumer writes `QRCodeDecoder.TryDecode(bitmap, ...)` and a C# 12 or 13 consumer (net8.0's default) `QRCodeImageDecoder.TryDecode(bitmap, ...)`, from one source with no `#if`. The documentation shows the enclosing-class form first, because most consumers will see only that form for years, and the migration guide explains why the 1.x spelling can stop compiling on net8.0, so that it is not reported as a missing overload.

The packages ship in lockstep, from one tag and one release run. `Directory.Build.props` keeps its single `<Version>`, and on pack the `ProjectReference` from the rendering package to the core becomes a package dependency at that version. The release workflow's push glob already covered several packages. Prerelease versions are a manual edit, because `bump_version.cs` produces `X.Y.Z` only.

The split came first and the renames second, with previews in between. The split is structural and touches every file. The 2.0.0 type renames are textual and touch every consumer. Together they would have produced a diff nobody could review. The split shipped as `2.0.0-preview.1` to claim the three IDs and exercise the pipeline, and the repository rename as `2.0.0-preview.2` to prove Trusted Publishing under the new name. The type renames followed in `2.0.0-preview.3`.

The repository followed the brand, and the Playground URL needed its own handling. GitHub redirects the web URL and every `git` operation from the old name indefinitely, as long as the old name is never reused, with GitHub Pages project sites the documented exception. The old Playground URL is printed in every 1.x package's README on nuget.org, which cannot be edited, and a path with no project site behind it falls through to the user site, so `SkiaSharp.QrCode/index.html` (and `api/index.html`) on `guitarrapc/guitarrapc.github.io` serve the old URLs and forward them by script, keeping the query and the hash (where shared Playground links keep their settings), with a meta refresh as the fallback when script does not run. A repository under the old name to host the stub was ruled out, since it would have broken the repository redirect. The nuget.org Trusted Publishing policy, bound to the owner and repository name, was updated in the same window.

### Why separate entry points instead of extending `Create`

The existing parameters do not generalize:

| Parameter | Standard QR | Micro QR | rMQR |
|---|---|---|---|
| Version | `int` 1–40 | M1–M4 | R7x43–R17x139 (32 rectangular sizes) |
| ECC level | L/M/Q/H | Detection only on M1, L/M on M2–M3, L/M/Q on M4 | M/H only |
| Auto-selection | Smallest version | Smallest version, mode legality varies per version | Fit strategy is two-dimensional (width-first vs height-first) |

Overloading one method family with union-typed parameters would make illegal combinations representable and push validation to runtime. Separate entry points make each symbology's constraints visible in the type system.

### Why sibling namespaces instead of a polymorphic abstraction

The Standard QR pipeline is heavily performance-tuned (zero-allocation steady state, SIMD kernels, stackalloc buffers, aggressive inlining). A shared abstraction over the pipeline stages (virtual dispatch, interface indirection, or generic strategy types) would put abstraction cost on the hot path and tie all symbologies to one pipeline shape, though their stages differ: rMQR has no mask selection, Micro QR has no interleaving for most versions, and format information differs in size, location and BCH code.

Sibling namespaces instead keep a Micro QR change from touching Standard QR code paths. The regression guard is structural (the namespace dependency rule) and empirical (Standard QR benchmarks must stay flat through every phase).

### Why `QRCodeData` is not generalized

`QRCodeData` is a shipped public type whose contract is square, 21–177 modules, versions 1–40, with a serialization format that encodes exactly that. Generalizing it would either break the serialization contract or turn every member into a symbology-conditional. Sibling data types keep the shipped contract byte-for-byte stable and let rectangular geometry be designed without compatibility constraints.

### When Kanji mode is written

All three decoders read Kanji mode, an interoperability obligation: Japanese-market encoders emit it, and a decoder that rejects those symbols leaves callers no way through.

Since 2.0.0 all three generators also write it on request (`AllowKanji` on each generator's options, off by default) for one class of text: the library chose the charset and chose UTF-8 (`EciMode.Default`, and on Standard QR no byte order mark), and every character is ASCII or has an encoder cell. The encoder cells are JIS X 0208 without the seven cells CP932 reads differently. When every character has a cell, the text goes out as one Kanji segment with no ECI header under both segmentations. When some characters are ASCII, `Single` writes UTF-8 as before, because one segment cannot hold both, while `Optimal` considers a Kanji plan (Kanji runs beside Numeric, Alphanumeric and Byte runs for the ASCII, with no ECI header) and takes it where it needs a smaller version than the UTF-8 stream. Every other text, and every text without the option, is written as before, bit for bit.

Why this rule and not a wider one:

- Kanji mode is written only on request. During 2.0.0's development, though in no release, the generators wrote it unasked. Scanned from a screen on 2026-10-01, an Android 17 phone's own QR scanner and Google Lens on that phone read nothing from a Kanji-mode Standard QR symbol, with or without ECI 20, and both read the same text as UTF-8 behind ECI 26. The iPhone camera, Google Lens on iPhone, ZXing, zxing-cpp, CodeGlyphX and Denso Wave's reader read both. A default that half the phones misread is not a default, so UTF-8 is the default on all three symbologies, and Kanji mode is for callers who know their readers or need the capacity. Neither phone's own scanner reads Micro QR or rMQR, and Denso Wave's reader and zxing-cpp read them in Kanji mode and UTF-8 alike, so nothing measured set them apart, and one rule for all three is the simpler contract.

- It reaches the texts UTF-8 served worst and never grows a symbol. A character with a cell costs 13 bits in Kanji mode against 16 or 24 in UTF-8, and the stream drops the 12-bit (rMQR 11-bit) ECI header. ASCII and ISO-8859-1 output never changes. On Micro QR, which has no ECI, Kanji mode is also the standard's own way to carry the text, where its UTF-8 was bare bytes a reader had to recognise.
- A charset the caller chose is honoured: explicit UTF-8, or a byte order mark (in effect a request for UTF-8), keeps UTF-8 with or without the option. Micro QR has no charset option. `AllowKanji` is its one switch.
- The seven divergent cells are never written. Whichever reading is written at one, a CP932 reader (ZXing.Net) and this library decode it to different text, so neither reading has an encoder cell, and a text that holds one stays UTF-8.
- No Kanji segment is written beside an ECI header. A text that would need both (a character without a cell next to characters with one) stays UTF-8. ISO/IEC 18004:2015 treats an ECI as governing the bytes of every mode, and Kanji mode compacts Shift_JIS-range byte pairs (7.4.2.1, 7.3.6, Annex H), so a Kanji segment after ECI 26 means UTF-8 bytes, not JIS X 0208 characters. Readers differ: zxing-cpp and ZBar follow the standard, while ZXing and its ports read JIS X 0208 there by their maintainer's choice. On 2026-10-01 (`spot-check-kanji`), zxing-cpp 0.5.2 returned replacement characters for such a segment and ISO-8859-1 for a Kanji segment ahead of the ECI, so no segment order avoids the problem. The rule was decided with the user the same day.
- Kanji segments carry no ECI. Every reader that decodes text reads a Kanji segment with no ECI as Shift_JIS, on both sides of that split. Strictly, the default interpretation has been ISO-8859-1 since the 2006 edition, and zint warns on Kanji without ECI 20. ECI 20 would remove that doubt at 12 bits per symbol, but the phone that reads no Kanji mode (Android 17) read no ECI 20 Kanji either, so the symbol stays without one.
- The rule is about what can be represented, not about script: Greek, Cyrillic and box drawing in JIS X 0208 go out in Kanji mode like kana do.
- `Optimal` never grows a symbol either. Like any plan, the Kanji plan is taken only below the version the single-mode stream needs, and the UTF-8 plan `Optimal` wrote before competes with it at every version. Interleaved kanji and digits pay a segment header per run as Kanji runs, so one UTF-8 Byte run can be the smaller plan there. At a version where both fit, the Kanji plan is written.

A Structured Append set follows the same rule for the whole text, and an eligible set has no ECI header in any symbol. Its parity, the XOR of the whole text's Shift_JIS bytes (an ASCII character counts as its byte), does not depend on the plan, so it is still fixed before the text is split. Under `Single` the set is a Kanji set only when every character has a cell, each chunk one Kanji segment. Under `Optimal`, a text with ASCII becomes a Kanji set, each chunk its Kanji plan, only when that set needs fewer symbols than the UTF-8 set, or as many at a lower version, so `Optimal` never gives a larger set than before. A text whose every character has a cell is a Kanji set under both, since its Kanji set is never the larger. A text that fits one symbol, judged as `Create` judges it, gets `Create`'s symbol.

`Decode(Encode(x)) == x` holds for Kanji output as for any other, and ZXing.Net and zxing-cpp read it. `Encode(Decode(y))` reproduces a Kanji symbol `y` only when `y` is what this library writes for its text. Symbols other encoders write with Kanji beside an ECI header, with CP932 readings, or with a split this library would not choose are read but not reproduced. The Kanji capacity columns are now encoding capacities, checked at every version and level of each symbology in the `*BinaryEncoderKanjiTest` classes.

The mapping is JIS X 0208, not CP932. The two disagree on seven Shift_JIS cells (0x815F, 0x8160, 0x8161, 0x817C, 0x8191, 0x8192, 0x81CA: reverse solidus, wave dash, double vertical line, minus sign, and the cent / pound / not signs), and within the Kanji-mode range CP932 also assigns 83 characters the standard does not, all NEC row 13 (0x8740-0x879C: circled digits, roman numerals, unit ligatures). CP932 would have mangled the characters Japanese payloads use in URLs and price strings. The shared `ShiftJisKanjiTable` holds only the 6,879-cell JIS X 0208 repertoire. Cells outside it are reported as `DecodeStatus.UnmappedCharacter` rather than replaced, so a corrupt symbol never becomes a plausible wrong answer, and a caller can tell "a CP932 reader would read this" apart from the structural `UnsupportedContent` cases (FNC1, unmapped ECI). The table costs 16 KB of RVA data, shared by all three symbologies, with no allocation and no static constructor.

The table is derived from a measurement and gated by arithmetic, not transcribed. Its values come from a sweep of every structurally valid Kanji-mode cell (8,023 of them, encoded by qrtool as raw Shift_JIS and read back by zxing-cpp), and the generator refuses to emit the table unless the swept data reproduces JIS X 0208's published repertoire size and differs from CP932 by exactly the documented divergence set. Reproducing 6,879 assigned cells independently (524 non-kanji + 6,355 kanji) makes "this is JIS X 0208" a measurement, not an assumption. Every other table test constrains only which cells are assigned and would pass permuted readings, so a golden digest over all 8,192 entries checks the values. Regenerating the table is expected to change the digest in the same reviewed commit.

The encoder's reverse table is the forward table's inverse, minus seven cells. `ShiftJisKanjiReverseTable` maps a UTF-16 code unit to the 13-bit value of its cell and holds 6,872 of them: the 6,879 above without the seven divergent cells, which have no cell to write. The same generator emits the reverse table from the forward table, and refuses unless, over every UTF-16 code unit, the reverse table is the exact inverse of the forward table on those cells and finds nothing for everything else, both readings of the seven included. A golden digest over all 65,536 lookups checks it, as the forward table's digest checks that one.

Its layout was chosen by measurement (2026-09-29, .NET 10, x64, 1,000 characters of Japanese prose and the 6,872 cells shuffled): a directory over the high byte, a 10-byte record per 64 code units (a membership word and the count of members before it), and the values in code-unit order, packed at 13 bits, for 15,146 bytes of RVA data and 2 to 3 ns per character. The alternatives measured:
- Binary search over sorted pairs: 27 KB and 14 ns.
- A perfect hash checked through the forward table: 14 KB and 7 ns.
- Unpacked 16-bit values: 17.7 KB, over the 16 KB target, and not consistently faster (9 % ahead on prose in one run, 26 % behind in the other, level on the shuffled cells in both).
- The word and its count in separate arrays, so that a lookup touches two tables for them instead of one record: 3 to 27 % slower.

Removing the bounds checks gained 0.2 to 0.5 ns, not worth unsafe code.

The trimmed cost of Kanji encoding was measured with `PublishTrimmed`, `TrimMode=full`, win-x64 on 2026-09-29, against the commit before any encoder referenced the table: QR encode only went from 115,200 to 132,608 bytes of `FeatherQR.dll` (+17.0 KB) and all three symbologies encoding from 178,176 to 197,120 (+18.5 KB), the 15.1 KB table plus the writers and the eligibility pass, while decode only stayed at 73,216. A decode-only consumer keeps no table it does not use, but an encoding consumer keeps the reverse table whether or not its text ever reaches Kanji mode, because the writers' mode switches reference it. Later changes:
- Kanji plans under `Optimal` (the eighth segmentation state, each planner's Kanji scan) added 4.5 KB more to QR encode only (137,216 bytes) and 7.0 KB to all three (204,288), measured 2026-09-30. A consumer that never sets `Optimal` keeps them too, since the segmentation is a run-time option.
- Kanji sets in Structured Append cost a consumer that calls `CreateStructuredAppend` 4.0 KB (161,792 → 165,888 bytes), and the others at most 0.5 KB (QR encode only 137,216 unchanged, all three 204,288 → 204,800), measured the same day.
- Making Kanji mode opt-in (`AllowKanji`, 2026-10-01) removed none of it, since the option is read at run time: all three 205,312 bytes and `CreateStructuredAppend` 166,400 (+0.5 KB each), QR encode only and decode only unchanged.
- Speeding up Kanji plans (a membership test for the analysis, the scan's table kept for the build, 2026-10-01) added 1.0 KB to QR encode only (138,240) and to `CreateStructuredAppend` (167,424), and 1.5 KB to all three (206,848). Decode only was unchanged.

Two failure causes are kept apart on the error path: a structurally impossible byte pair is `InvalidBitstream`, and a well-formed but unassigned cell is `UnmappedCharacter`. The arithmetic that tells them apart runs on the error path only, so the happy path stays a single indexed load.

On the image path, `UnmappedCharacter` and `UnsupportedContent` are verdicts on the symbol's content, reached only after its error correction, and one is reported when no attempt reads a symbol. The first attempt and the inverted retry run as they always have, so a readable symbol elsewhere in the image (a light-on-dark one beside it, say) is still read. A verdict from either skips the regional pass, which looks for a symbol the global threshold cannot see, so a second, unevenly lit symbol beside one that gave a verdict is not looked for. In the regional pass, a verdict on the positive ends the pass before the negative.

Inside an attempt, a verdict counts like a read wherever Standard QR chooses between grids for one symbol (the timing frame or the finder grid, other dimensions, the mesh or the global grid, the finder-only grid, the mirrored grid), whichever grid reached it. Micro QR and rMQR rank a verdict above a correction failure on another grid for the same symbol, and report a verdict that their full finder sweep reaches. Their scans still try every remaining candidate after a verdict, and a verdict from the strided scan still runs the full sweep, which can find another symbol that reads.

When every attempt fails short of the content, the first attempt's diagnostics are reported. `DataUncorrectable` and `InvalidBitstream` stay out of that rule, since noise reaches the first and a miscorrection the second. A failed decode, of an image or a matrix, reports no characters written, whatever it left in the destination. The matrix overloads do so since 2.0.0. Before, one that failed partway through the bit stream counted the segments it had written, and only the image overloads reported none.

ECI 20 (Shift_JIS) byte-mode segments, which need the wider CP932 single-byte plus double-byte range, and (Standard QR) FNC1 are still unsupported and reported as `UnsupportedContent`. Structured Append is read and written since 2.0.0 (Standard QR only, see [standardqr-decoder.md](standardqr-decoder.md) and [standardqr-encoder.md](standardqr-encoder.md)).

### Allocation contract

The span-destination overloads are documented as allocating nothing per call, not as never touching the heap: every symbology builds immutable lookup tables lazily on first use and caches them for the process (the per-version placement and extraction layouts and, on ARM64, a 24 KB alpha-step table shared by all three symbologies, because there the syndrome kernel reads its data terms from a table rather than computing them). They are built once, keyed by version, published with a release store, and bounded (about 100 KB if every rMQR version were exercised). An allocation benchmark must warm up first, or it charges that one-time build to the call that triggered it.

A test checks the promise, not a reading of the code. `DecodeAllocationTest` decodes through every allocation-free overload of the three decoders: the matrix overloads with and without a quiet zone, and the image overloads on each path the image level reads through (upright, turned, mirrored, keystone, the next finder triple, the meshes, the timing frame, low density, the anisotropic grid, the perspective search, light on dark, uneven light) and on images that fail (noise, another symbology's symbol). It also counts how many of Standard QR's module buffers are out at once, which is one. It caught an allocation planted at each stage of both levels, 47 of them (2026-09-29). Measuring it taught four things:

- Allocation is measured in Release only. Debug allocates where Release does not: a span initialized from a list of literals (`stackalloc float[] { … }`, `ReadOnlySpan<int> x = [ … ]`) allocated 72 B per call unoptimized. A file-based script (`dotnet run script.cs`) runs in Release only with `-c Release` on the command line. A `#:property Configuration=Release` directive alone still gave the 72 B.
- The test warms up, then takes the quietest of a few rounds. The shared array pool can drop a buffer when a garbage collection runs, so in one round a single rent can allocate, while a call that allocates every time does so in every round.
- Such a test runs alone (`[NotInParallel]`). The pool's per-thread slot holds one array of each size, and a second array of that size comes from per-core stacks, which tests running alongside can drain. That is how Standard QR's nested module buffers showed up, as 4,120 B on noise in one run of six, before each scan held only one ([standardqr-decoder.md](standardqr-decoder.md), Performance).
- A planted allocation has to escape. `GC.KeepAlive(new byte[1])` is caught where `new byte[1].Length` at the same stage was not (.NET 10), because an array that never leaves the method need not be allocated.

### SIMD tier inventory

[SimdTiers.cs](../../../src/FeatherQR/Internals/SimdTiers.cs) is the one table of which SIMD tier each kernel runs on each build, and real builds are checked against it. For each kernel it lists the tiers in dispatch order, each tier's condition, and the tier the kernel runs on each build class. [qrcode-simd-tiers.md](qrcode-simd-tiers.md) shows the rendered table, the builds in each of the four build classes and a key to the tiers. A new symbology or kernel should reuse the shared kernels in the table rather than reimplement them.

Each build also reports what it runs: `tests/FeatherQR.AotAnalysis` (native builds) and `tests/FeatherQR.WasmReport` (WebAssembly, run under Node.js, which has a browser's WebAssembly SIMD) print the instruction sets the build and the CPU provide, and each kernel's tiers with the one it runs. With `--simd-class` they fail when the build disagrees with the table.

A cell gives one tier, or, where an instruction set depends on the CPU in that build class, the tiers the CPU chooses between, of which exactly one runs on any one machine. When the table was first drawn (2026-09-28), 11 of the 28 kernels ran scalar on x64 without AVX, 2 on x64 with AVX2, 1 on ARM64 and 19 on WebAssembly, and more on CPUs without GFNI, fast PEXT or the ARM64 dot-product instructions (`Dp`).

Since the 128-bit round below (2026-10-01), only the Structured Append parity and scanner on x64, the rMQR value writers and (since the Standard QR payload writers of 2026-10-05) those writers on ARM64, and seven kernels on WebAssembly (six before them) run scalar, each with its measured reason next to its row, and no cell drops to scalar because the CPU lacks a feature. The netstandard builds have no intrinsics, so they run scalar everywhere. Which instruction set a NativeAOT publish should target is a separate decision, to which the table is an input ([NativeAOT's instruction-set target](#nativeaots-instruction-set-target)).

These keep the table accurate:

- Each dispatch reads its own flags, and a source test ties the table to them. `SimdTiersTest` checks that every instruction-set flag a kernel's files read is the condition of a tier the table declares for that kernel, that every declared tier's flags are read there, that each tier's condition reads its own flags, and that no other file reads one (`HardwareCapabilities` aside), though not the order in which a dispatch tries its tiers. The dispatch does not read the table, because the JIT inlines a dispatch into its caller only when it reads `IsSupported` directly (Lessons learned).
- The table states the exact tier, not a minimum. A minimum would let an understating table pass (a kernel gains a tier, or loses its GFNI tier on a runner that has GFNI), and a plain snapshot would flap, because hosted runners change CPUs between jobs. `SimdTierTableTest` checks the table in every CPU state each class allows, on any machine, ARM64 and WebAssembly included. It also checks that removing the tier a kernel runs fails the check in every state where that tier was chosen, the change the source test misses when the code and the declaration lose the tier together. It checks the test process against its own class too, so every test leg checks its JIT.
- CI runs every build class. The `aot-analysis` job publishes the NativeAOT gate as the default linux-x64 build, an `x86-64-v3` build, and the default build on linux-arm64, win-arm64 and osx-arm64, and runs each with `--simd-class`. It also runs the JIT on the same runners with `DOTNET_EnableAVX=0` on x64 and `DOTNET_EnableArm64Dp=0` on ARM64, for the side of a class the runner's CPU does not show. The linux-x64 runner had no GFNI when the job first ran (2026-09-28), so the GFNI side of the x64 cells has only run on a developer machine.
  - The `wasm-simd` job runs the WebAssembly report interpreted and AOT-compiled, as a headless report of its own. Reading it from the Playground would need a browser and would put the library's internals into an app that ships.
  - Both jobs also pass `--parity`, which checks every vector tier against its scalar form on random inputs, NaN and out-of-range coordinates included, in the code the build emitted. It is the only output check for `PackedSimd` operations and ILC's code. The JIT runs with the knobs pass it too, since the test suite covers only the side of a class the runner's CPU picks.
- A file's name says which instruction families it may use: `{stem}.X86.cs` x86 intrinsics and the vectors they work on, `{stem}.Arm64.cs` ARM intrinsics on 128-bit vectors, `{stem}.Vector256.cs` and `{stem}.Vector128.cs` portable vectors of that width or narrower, and `{stem}.Simd.cs` a tier that picks its instructions per instruction set inside one method (WebAssembly's `PackedSimd` among them). The stem file holds the entry point, the dispatch and the scalar tier, and uses no vector instructions. Tiers move between files only as whole methods (Lessons learned). Six stem files keep a tier inline, where an entry point the scalar build also runs holds the vector steps next to the scalar tail they hand over to. `SimdLayoutTest.InlineTiers` lists them and where the tier sits, and fails when one stops being inline or another file starts.
- The rendered tables follow the code. `SimdTiersDocTest` renders the tables in [qrcode-simd-tiers.md](qrcode-simd-tiers.md) from `SimdTiers.cs`, fails when the file differs, and checks that the document's key lists every tier. Outside CI it also rewrites them, so a change to the table shows up as a diff to commit.
- A new kernel, tier or build class fails the tests until every piece is in place: a kernel needs its row in the table and its files in `SimdTiersTest`, a tier its key row in qrcode-simd-tiers.md, and a build class its name in `SimdTiersDocTest`.

#### The 128-bit round

From 2026-09-29 to 2026-10-01, every scalar cell on x64 without AVX (a default NativeAOT publish) and on WebAssembly got a portable `Vector128` tier wherever one beat what that build was running. Elsewhere the cell kept its measured reason. A tier shipped only under these rules, which still apply to new ones:

- It beats what the build runs, measured on that build, and loses nowhere beyond noise. A kernel under about 3 % of every benchmark shape on a build is left as it is there, with its measured reason next to its row. The bar is on the kernel's share, not on what a step is estimated to save. Over it, the step is built and measured end to end, and where its gain is the size of the runs' spread, the stage rows (the kernel alone over the encode) give the gain's size. Interpreted and AOT-compiled WebAssembly run the same tier, so the rule has to hold on both. Most Blazor apps run interpreted.
- It is portable `Vector128`, and an operation slow on one build may use that platform's instruction behind its `IsSupported` check (x86 on a default NativeAOT publish, `PackedSimd` on WebAssembly), kept only where it wins. There is no 128-bit GFNI tier: it would fill the x64 cell only on GFNI CPUs and do nothing for WebAssembly.
- A step only WebAssembly needs is gated on `PackedSimd.IsSupported`, which is constant false elsewhere. Gated on `Vector128.IsHardwareAccelerated` instead, it would be compiled into a default NativeAOT publish, where its SSSE3 check runs at run time.
- Its output matches the scalar tier's. A parity test calls the tier directly, because the dispatch hides a lower tier behind a higher one, and planted faults make that test fail. `--parity` checks the code each CI build emitted, through the tier's own entry point, NaN and out-of-range input included.
- Its machine code is read, not only timed. Cells that did not change compile as before, and moving code between methods or files costs no instructions, on the JIT (.NET 8 and 10 on x64 with and without AVX and on ARM64) and on ILC (default x64, `x86-64-v3`, ARM64).
- Both .NET targets compile it. An operation .NET 8 lacks (`ShuffleNative`, `AddSaturate`, `NarrowWithSaturation`, `MinNative`) gets a .NET 8 version, or the .NET 8 build keeps its old tier. No public API was added, and nothing allocates.

Each build was measured running as itself: `--time` in both report projects times the benchmark shapes end to end and each kernel alone, through its dispatch and its scalar entry point, each shape in its own process, alternating between builds. x64 without AVX was measured as a default NativeAOT publish, because the JIT under `DOTNET_EnableAVX=0` compiles portable vectors as `x86-64-v2` does, not as a default publish does, and ARM64 without the dot-product instructions as a NativeAOT build with `IlcInstructionSet=armv8-a,-dotprod`. A kernel's share is its time alone divided by the shape's time.

The table gives the branch's end-to-end time divided by main's (1cf1436, with Kanji encoding and the shared Micro QR and rMQR decode pipeline), measured 2026-10-02 with each shape in its own process and five alternations, or eleven for any shape that measured above 1.00:

| Shapes | win-x64 NativeAOT | linux-x64 NativeAOT | WebAssembly AOT | WebAssembly interpreted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Matrix decode (10) | 0.20 to 0.91 | 0.21 to 0.86 | 0.24 to 0.88 | 0.32 to 0.96 |
| Image decode (14) | 0.20 to 0.95 | 0.21 to 0.96 | 0.17 to 0.52 | 0.28 to 0.87 |
| Bitmap decode (2) | 0.20 to 0.27 | 0.22 to 0.27 | 0.30 to 0.48 | 0.40 to 0.48 |
| Data-object API (4) | 0.25 to 1.02 | 0.23 to 1.00 | 0.30 to 0.86 | 0.46 to 0.95 |
| Encode (18) | 0.62 to 1.01 | 0.66 to 1.00 | 0.49 to 0.99 | 0.51 to 1.00 |
| Kanji encode (2) | 0.99 to 1.00 | 1.00 | 0.97 to 0.98 | 0.96 |

The Kanji encodes are Standard QR with `AllowKanji`: 200 chars that all have a Kanji cell under `Single`, and 400 chars of Kanji and ASCII under `Optimal`. The cells above 1.00 come from three small encodes on win-x64 (Micro QR M3 and two rMQR shapes at 1.01 to 1.02, 2 to 25 ns longer than main's), whose methods ILC compiles to the same instructions as main's or fewer (rMQR's format placement) and which measure 0.95 to 0.97 on linux-x64, so the difference is code placement. On ARM64 (Apple M2, measured 2026-10-01 against main at 3e1f29d), where the round changed one cell, the end-to-end shapes measure 0.87 to 1.02 with the dot-product instructions, on NativeAOT and on the JIT, and the bitmap decodes 0.57 to 0.69 without them.

Each kernel's results are in its symbology's record:
- the edge list, the histogram, the samplers, the syndromes and the search levels in [standardqr-decoder.md](standardqr-decoder.md)
- mask selection, the Structured Append walks and the Reed-Solomon encoder in [standardqr-encoder.md](standardqr-encoder.md)
- the extraction and the luminance in [rmqr-decoder.md](rmqr-decoder.md)
- the placer and the value writers in [rmqr-encoder.md](rmqr-encoder.md)

Three shared kernels have no record of their own, so their results are here:

- `TextAnalyzer` on WebAssembly, 16 chars per step, is 2.7 to 12x faster than scalar on 2,900 chars. A block with a char above U+00FF determines every flag, so wherever the tier narrows chars to bytes, the narrowing is exact. The dispatch uses the tier only for texts of 32 chars or more: interpreted, the tier costs about 0.2 µs on any text up to 24 chars, 1.6x the scalar pass at 8 chars, and is level or better from 32. The smallest encodes showed that cost (1.03 to 1.09 interpreted) until the threshold moved from 8 to 32 at the end of the round.
- `ModuleBitPacker` on WebAssembly, using the swizzle for the byte reversal, is 2.2 to 4.1x faster. Only the data-object API packs and unpacks, so the span API's shapes never showed it.
- `ModeSegmenter`'s lanes on x64 without AVX and on WebAssembly are the ARM64 four-lane groups on portable vectors, so those builds now plan a set's symbols together too, which moved a set's time by 1 to 3 %.

#### The ARM64 queue

Some work already helps every target, whatever its SIMD: cached per-version layouts, pair stores and index scatter, table-driven auto-fit, the portable extraction walk, the safe finder stride with a full-sweep retry, sub-finder guards, and Otsu reuse.

The ARM64 optimization queue is closed. Four components were measured and left out of it: Otsu histogramming (serial histogram updates, already near its measured per-pixel floor), the sub-finder and perspective search (branchy, data-dependent and dominated by the failure path), rendering and PNG encoding (dominated by Skia's native code), and the 1.3-8.3 ns version selector. ARM64 work reopens only when a new profile points to a different mechanism, which has happened three times, each time followed by closing the queue again:

- On 2026-09-21, a stage profile of the Standard QR matrix decode on Apple M2 pointed to the syndrome pass's carried dependency chain, and the shared AdvSimd kernel was re-associated to eight bytes per step.
- On 2026-09-22, an image-decode stage profile on Apple M2 put the histogram fill at 30-87 % of a version 40 decode, because the same-bin increment chain costs this core twice what it costs x64. The fill now has an ARM64 tier that counts block extremes without a movemask and spreads dense blocks over four sub-histograms, which this core's L1 holds and x64's did not, so the Otsu entry's "near the per-pixel floor" reason no longer stands.
- Also on 2026-09-22, after the fill's tier, the profile pointed to the finder search's mask walk (10 to 50 % of a version 40 decode, 46 % of an image with no symbol, bound by its branches as on x64), and then to the mesh sampler's column-table tier (45 µs of a 138 µs decode). Both now have ARM64 tiers: the row kernel builds its word from the NEON fold, eight windows per step, and the sampler runs on four lanes, two steps per loop body. The x64 round's findings carried over as structure, not as instructions, and each tier was tuned again on the M2 against its own reference.

The details are in the Performance lessons of [standardqr-decoder.md](standardqr-decoder.md). WebAssembly and x64 without AVX ran the scalar fill, the column table and the 128-bit mask walk until the 128-bit round gave them 128-bit tiers for the fill, the mesh sampler and the edge list, each measured on those builds.

#### NativeAOT's instruction-set target

A NativeAOT publish compiles for the instruction sets its target names, and the default target is the OS's minimum, so on x64 it runs the tiers of a CPU without AVX on every CPU. [What .NET gives each build](qrcode-simd-tiers.md#what-net-gives-each-build) lists what each target gives. A probe through `tests/FeatherQR.AotAnalysis` found the following, on the development box (Ryzen 9 7950X3D, win-x64, ILCompiler 10.0.9, 2026-10-02) and on an Apple M2 (linux-arm64, SDK 10.0.401 with ILCompiler 10.0.12, 2026-10-03):

- A targeted instruction set is required, not checked per use. On a CPU without it the NativeAOT runtime prints "The required instruction sets are not supported by the current CPU." at startup and exits non-zero before any user code runs (probed with `x86-64-v3,avx10v1` on a Zen 4, which has no AVX10).
- Sets outside the target are checked at run time: GFNI under `x86-64-v3`, and SSSE3 to SSE4.2 and GFNI under the default. A target of `x86-64-v4` or `native` also makes AVX-512 read true.
- With AVX in the target (`x86-64-v2,avx`, the comma passed as `%2C` on a command line), `Avx2`, `Bmi2` and `Gfni` become run-time checks, but `Vector256.IsHardwareAccelerated` reads false. The 11 kernels gated on `Avx2`, `Avx2Pext` or `GfniV256` (`TextAnalyzer`, `ModuleBitPacker`, `EccBinaryEncoder`, `EccBinaryDecoder`, `LuminanceConverter`, `ModulePlacerExpandBits`, `ModulePlacerMaskCode`, `QRSampleGridPiecewise`, `MicroQRModulePlacer`, `RmQRModulePlacer`, `RmQRExtractCodewords`) then take their `x86-64-v3` tiers. The 8 gated on `Vector256` (`ModeSegmenterLanes`, `LuminanceInverter`, `Binarizer`, `FinderRowMask`, `FinderRowEdges`, `PerspectiveGridSampler`, `AlignmentRowMask`, `StructuredAppendLanes`) keep their 128-bit tiers, and the other 9 take the same tier in all three targets. So the encode side gets its AVX2 tiers back and most of the image decode does not.
- On ARM64 the JIT and a default NativeAOT publish see the same sets (AdvSimd and the dot product) and take the same tier in all 28 kernels, so a default publish loses no tier. NativeAOT ignores `DOTNET_EnableArm64Dp`, so only a publish for `armv8-a,-dotprod` shows a CPU without the dot product.

The [cross-language benchmark](qrcode-cross-language-benchmark.md) measured the gap on the development box (linux-x64 in Docker, 2026-10-03, two runs of five rounds), each entry's ratio the geometric mean of its two runs, median and range by shape. The JIT without AVX takes exactly default NativeAOT's tiers (both printed the same instruction sets in every process), so it separates what the lost tiers cost from what ahead-of-time code costs, without a second compiler:

| Shape | Lost tiers (JIT without AVX over JIT) | Ahead-of-time code (default NativeAOT over JIT without AVX) | Default NativeAOT over JIT | `x86-64-v3` NativeAOT over JIT | Default over `x86-64-v3` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Standard QR encode | 1.62 (1.59 to 1.78) | 1.23 | 2.00 (1.95 to 2.18) | 1.23 | 1.61 (1.59 to 1.76) |
| Standard QR matrix decode | 1.10 | 1.16 | 1.27 | 1.10 | 1.14 |
| Standard QR image decode | 1.19 | 1.15 | 1.37 | 1.08 | 1.26 |
| Micro QR encode | 1.22 (1.04 to 1.31) | 1.04 | 1.21 (1.09 to 1.36) | 1.09 | 1.11 |
| Micro QR matrix decode | 1.09 | 0.93 | 1.03 | 0.99 | 1.03 |
| Micro QR image decode | 1.17 | 1.14 | 1.34 | 1.10 | 1.21 |
| rMQR encode | 1.12 (1.05 to 1.27) | 1.04 | 1.17 (1.10 to 1.27) | 1.06 | 1.11 |
| rMQR matrix decode | 1.16 (1.14 to 1.36) | 1.11 | 1.31 (1.26 to 1.49) | 1.22 | 1.04 (1.04 to 1.33) |
| rMQR image decode | 1.22 | 1.20 | 1.46 (1.40 to 1.56) | 1.13 | 1.28 |

The two causes multiply: Standard QR encode loses 1.62 to its tiers and 1.23 to ahead-of-time code, and runs at 2.00. A publish for `x86-64-v3` removes the first and leaves the second, 0.99 to 1.26 over the JIT by entry and 1.10 at the median, which is code compiled once without the JIT's tiered recompilation and dynamic PGO. The table's encodes predate the change that stopped a pinned encode from analysing its text twice ([standardqr-encoder.md](standardqr-encoder.md)), and the runners' figures below include it. On hosted runners (2026-10-06, one run of five rounds) default NativeAOT ran 1.0 to 1.9 times the JIT by shape on an EPYC 7763 (Standard QR encode 1.9) and `x86-64-v3` 1.0 to 1.2. On a Neoverse-N2, and on the Apple M2, where no tier is lost, default NativeAOT ran 1.0 to 1.2 times the JIT.

The kernels behind the default arm's gap, by shape, are those each shape's clean path reaches that change tier between the two targets. Every one falls to a 128-bit tier, and none to scalar:

| Shape | Kernels that change tier, `x86-64-v3` to default |
|---|---|
| Standard QR encode | `TextAnalyzer` (`Avx2` to `Sse2`), `ModulePlacerExpandBits` and `ModulePlacerMaskCode` (`Avx2` to `Ssse3`). `EccBinaryEncoder` (`GfniV256` to `Gfni`) only where a block has more than 16 ECC codewords |
| Micro QR encode | `TextAnalyzer`, `MicroQRModulePlacer` (`Avx2Pext` to `Ssse3`), `ModuleBitPacker` (`Avx2` to `Ssse3`) |
| rMQR encode | `TextAnalyzer`, `RmQRModulePlacer` (`Avx2` to `Ssse3`), `ModuleBitPacker`, and `EccBinaryEncoder` where a block has more than 16 ECC codewords, here the R17x139 entry |
| Matrix decode, all three | `EccBinaryDecoder` (`GfniV256` to `Vector128`), and for rMQR `RmQRExtractCodewords` (`Avx2Pext` to `Vector128`) |
| Image decode, all three | `Binarizer` and `FinderRowEdges` (`Vector256` to `Vector128`), then the matrix decode's kernels. Standard QR adds `PerspectiveGridSampler` (`Vector256` to `Sse2`) and, from version 2, `AlignmentRowMask` (`Vector256` to `Vector128`) |

On the machines measured, NativeAOT starts and makes its first call in about 1 to 4 ms, against 17 to 45 ms to start and 9 to 68 ms for the first call under the JIT.

The library can change some of this and not the rest:

- The target is the application's compile setting, so no library-side switch reaches a default publish. What the library controls is its 128-bit tiers, which default NativeAOT, ARM64 and WebAssembly all run ([The 128-bit round](#the-128-bit-round)).
- Gating the eight `Vector256` kernels on `Avx2.IsSupported` instead might let an `x86-64-v2,avx` target run them at 256 bits. How ILC compiles portable `Vector256` operations when `Vector256` is not accelerated is unknown, so the disassembly comes first. Nothing was switched (2026-10-02).
- `x86-64-v2,avx` has not been timed on the current code. A rough timing before the 128-bit tiers found that it recovered most of the encode gap and almost none of the image decode gap. It is in none of `SimdTiers.cs`'s build classes, so `--simd-class` cannot check it.
- Selecting AVX and `Vector256` at run time needs the JIT (ReadyToRun included), or an application that ships a default and an `x86-64-v3` build and picks one at launch. Both are the application's choice.

## Scope decisions

| Decision | Choice | Revisit when |
|---|---|---|
| Package topology | `FeatherQR` (core) + `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` (renderer) + `SkiaSharp.QrCode` (empty metapackage). One core for all three symbologies, split at the leaf | Never for the core split itself. The metapackage is retired only after the last 1.x listing is gone from nuget.org |
| Per-symbology core packages | Rejected: it would save untrimmed consumers 100 to 130 KB of 384 KB at the cost of a four-package core with a public surface for the shared kernels, and trimmed consumers already get one symbology (95 KB for QR encode only) | Trimming stops being precise, which only a unified entry point could cause, and that is never added |
| Luminance conversion API | Internal (`LuminanceConverter.Convert` + `PixelLayout`), used by the first-party renderer through `InternalsVisibleTo`. Third parties decode through `TryDecodeImage` with their own luminance | A concrete request for a non-Skia first-class decode adapter. Promotion is a visibility change, since the adapter shape is already single-entry |
| `InternalsVisibleTo` from the core to `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` | Permanent for first-party packages. Every use is listed under "Package seam" with a replacement or a reason | A listed use gains a public replacement (the list shrinks). The grant itself stays |
| Pure-BCL SVG writer and 1-bit PNG writer in the core | Not built. They belong in the core (no Skia needed to emit either) and would let a `FeatherQR`-only consumer produce an image file | A request for image output without SkiaSharp. `GetModuleRectangles` already gives the geometry an SVG writer needs |
| Additional renderer packages (ImageSharp, System.Drawing, ...) | None. The split makes them possible: a renderer draws from `GetModuleRectangles` and decodes through `TryDecodeImage` | A request with a concrete consumer |
| The announced removals (`GetRequiredBufferSize`, `Compression`, parameter-list generator overloads) | Done in 2.0.0-preview.3. Every generator now takes only `in {Sym}CodeGeneratorOptions`, defaulted | Never. A throwing sizing method is asserted absent |
| 2.0.0 type renames (the `QR` casing rule, `ECCLevel` to `QREccLevel` and friends) and the `string` convenience overloads | Done in 2.0.0-preview.3, separately from the split: every public name follows the naming rule under "Public API direction", and the `string` overloads were dropped | - |
| Pages fallback stub on the user site | Kept for as long as 1.x packages are listed on nuget.org, since their READMEs link the old Playground URL | Never while a 1.x listing exists |
| Kanji mode (all symbologies) | Read with the JIS X 0208 mapping. Written on request (`AllowKanji`) when the charset is the library's choice ([When Kanji mode is written](#when-kanji-mode-is-written)): one Kanji segment for text whose every character has an encoder cell, and under `Optimal`, Kanji runs beside ASCII runs where that plan is smaller. Structured Append sets follow the same rule, with the Shift_JIS parity | Kanji beside an ECI header, if the readers that follow the standard there (zxing-cpp, ZBar) are measured to apply JIS X 0208 to it. Kanji mode by default, if an Android phone's own scanners are measured to read it |
| ECI 20 (Shift_JIS) byte segments | Unsupported, and reported as `UnsupportedContent` (structural, unlike the per-character `UnmappedCharacter`) | Demand for symbols that pair ECI 20 with Byte mode. It needs the full CP932 range, roughly twice the Kanji table |
| Image detection default | Standard QR only (`QRCodeDecoder`). Micro QR and rMQR scanning have their own explicitly typed entry points (`MicroQRCodeDecoder`, `RmQRCodeDecoder`). The Playground tries the three in that order | - |
| Shared detection primitives (Otsu, run-ratio scan) | Lifted to `Internals.ImageDecoders` when the Micro QR image decoder became their second consumer (2026-07-17) | - |
| `QRCodeData` | Frozen for Standard QR | Never (compatibility contract) |
| Interoperability runs against external encoders/decoders | Manual, not a CI job: `tools/QRInteropFixtures` spot-checks (`spot-check-rmqr`, `spot-check-microqr`) are run by hand before a release, and pull-request CI stays self-contained on the committed fixture corpus | A regression the committed corpus cannot catch, or an external oracle that installs cleanly enough for scheduled CI under the pinning policy in [qrcode-test-fixtures.md](qrcode-test-fixtures.md) |
| Physical scanner acceptance | Not automated and never a conformance gate: a disagreeing phone scanner proves an interoperability problem, never a specification violation. Run ad hoc against a representative print/screen set before a symbology's first release | A field report that the committed corpus and the image-degradation tests both pass but real scanners fail |
| SIMD tier table | One table in `Internals/SimdTiers.cs`, per kernel and build class, checked by source and table tests and by every build class in CI. The dispatch keeps its own flag reads. Tiers move between files only as whole methods. Six are kept inline and listed | A JIT that inlines a dispatch through a property, which would let the dispatch read the table. A kept-inline tier rewritten as a method of its own for another reason |
| NativeAOT instruction-set target | The application's setting. On x64 the default target costs 1.03 to 2.00 times the JIT's time by shape and `x86-64-v3` 0.99 to 1.23, and on ARM64 the default loses no tier ([NativeAOT's instruction-set target](#nativeaots-instruction-set-target)). The README's NativeAOT section states this and when to target `x86-64-v3` (2026-10-06) | A .NET release that changes what a default publish targets, or a tier change that moves the gap |
| 128-bit tiers where x64 without AVX or WebAssembly runs scalar | Done for 2.0.0 (2026-10-01, the 128-bit round under the SIMD tier inventory), where one beats what the build ran, measured on that build. The Structured Append parity and scanner on x64, six kernels on WebAssembly and the rMQR value writers on ARM64 stay scalar (with the Standard QR Numeric writer of 2026-10-05, seven on WebAssembly), each with its reason beside its row | A new kernel or build class, or a profile that puts a scalar cell's kernel over the bar |

## Lessons learned

- A claim about consumer compilation cannot be checked from the library's own build, which compiles at C# 14 and proves nothing about what a consumer at the SDK-default language version can write: "`string` converts implicitly on all four target frameworks" was recorded as fact and is false for the netstandard2.0 asset. Checking such a claim needs a consumer project per target framework at the default language version, preferably one that also runs. The same measurement found that `init`-only options could not be configured there once the parameter lists were gone (see "Public API direction" above).
- A differential test dies with what it compares against. Three test classes proved the options overloads matched the released parameter lists, and deleting the lists would have left them comparing a call with itself, so the output of every configuration was captured from the released overloads just before the removal and frozen as expected values (version, matrix size, SHA-256 of the serialized matrix and of the destination buffer), a stronger guarantee that catches an encoder change, not just two spellings disagreeing. The sizing sweeps were pointed at the encode itself instead: a buffer sized by `TryGetRequiredBufferSize` has to be the buffer `Create*` fills, the invariant a caller depends on. This had to be decided before deleting, since the values cannot be recovered after.

  The same sweep missed one test. `ArgumentErrorPrecedenceTest` compared the options path against the parameter-list path, and the sweep that removed the parameter lists (2026-09-06) rewrote the removed spelling into the surviving one instead of deleting the test, so on this branch, until the pre-PR review, it compared a call with a textually identical copy of itself. It reached no tag and no released package. Converting the three classes that were noticed did not make the rule hold. Only re-reading every test that named a removed member did.
- The two removed sizing overloads disagreed about exception types, frozen for two releases. This was measured rather than read from the docs, which had drifted: Standard QR reported a content overflow as `InvalidOperationException` and Micro QR the same condition as `ArgumentException`, and Standard QR reported an undefined `QREccLevel` as `ArgumentException`, where Micro QR and rMQR use `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. Both shipped in v1.1.1, so changing either was the break the deprecation window existed to avoid. An exception type is the one part of a public API no compiler checks, which is why it drifted and why the fix was a test rather than proofreading.
- `required` members put `[Obsolete]` on every constructor not annotated `[SetsRequiredMembers]`, and a metadata-level API listing shows that like a deprecation: in `PublicAPI.approved.txt`, `IconData` looked as if it carried an announced removal, which it does not. The marker is how the compiler stops a pre-C#-11 consumer from bypassing the required-member check. Check a listing entry against the source before acting on it.
- A blanket identifier rewrite reaches third-party API with the same spelling: renaming `ECCLevel` → `QREccLevel` also renamed `QRCoder.QRCodeGenerator.ECCLevel` in the comparator benchmarks, which only the compiler caught. A repository-wide rename of a common name has to be checked against the build, and a comparator benchmark is where the collision happens.
- PowerShell's `-ne` is case-insensitive, so `if ($new -ne $old) { write }` silently skips a case-only rename. `Internals.RmQr` → `Internals.RmQR` wrote nothing on the first pass, and only the compiler's "type does not exist" showed it. Case-only renames need `-cne`, and on a case-insensitive filesystem the directory needs two `git mv` steps.
- A removal is a rename in disguise, and the compiler finds only half of it. Deleting the parameter-list overloads broke 119 call sites the compiler reported and one it could not: `requestedVersion: -1` meant "automatic", while `QRVersionRange` rejects `-1` by design, so the mechanical rewrite compiled and threw at run time. The test suite caught it, as a consumer's would, which is why the migration guide leads with that trap rather than with the argument-to-property table.
- A blanket rename sweep also reaches this repository's own released package. `samples/Dotfiles/FinderPatternAlwaysBlack.cs` pins `#:package SkiaSharp.QrCode@1.0.0` as a bug repro, and the 2.0.0 rename sweep (2026-09-06) rewrote its calls to the unreleased 2.0.0 names, so a file that built on `main` no longer compiled against the package it names. It is the QRCoder lesson one directory over, and why that file now has a comment telling the next sweep to skip it. Nothing in CI builds `samples/Dotfiles`, so only a manual run found it.
- A case-only rename needs a case-sensitive oracle, and on Windows neither the filesystem nor `git status` is one. Twenty-nine spec-map links and one prose mention pointed at `Internals/StandardQr/` for three releases after that folder became `StandardQR`, because on a case-insensitive filesystem a link checker that resolves against the disk reports them all as fine. The rename that prompted the sweep, `Internals/RmQr` to `Internals/RmQR`, had left only one prose mention of its own. Resolving each link against `git ls-files` found the rest, and re-reading `git diff` before committing proved the fix was staged.

- ZXing.Net (the in-CI cross-validation oracle for Standard QR) cannot decode Micro QR or rMQR, so CI cannot cross-verify the new symbologies with it. Committed external fixtures are the primary conformance oracle instead. See [qrcode-test-fixtures.md](qrcode-test-fixtures.md).
- The Kanji divergence set is seven cells, not the six usually quoted. 0x815F (reverse solidus U+005C against fullwidth U+FF3C) is not on the commonly circulated list and does diverge, while 0x815C, which is on it, agrees (both U+2015). Building the override list from memory would have shipped two wrong cells. The sweep found both at once.
- CP932 does not report unassigned cells as unmapped: .NET returns U+30FB for them, so a naive "did it decode?" comparison counts 1,061 phantom assignments on top of the 83 real NEC row 13 characters. Any comparison against CP932 has to account for that, which is why the generator checks against published totals rather than filtering on whether a decode succeeded.
- NEC row 13 (0x8740-0x879C: circled digits, roman numerals, unit ligatures) came out cleanly under the same arithmetic: CP932 assigns 83 of its 92 structurally valid cells, zxing-cpp none, and excluding them makes the total come out at 6,879. So a symbol carrying `①` in Kanji mode is reported as unmapped rather than decoded under a mapping the standard does not define.
- `EncodingModeExtensions.GetCountIndicatorLength` looked shared but encodes Standard QR's version thresholds (10/27), while Micro QR and rMQR define their own indicator-width tables. The enum is shared. The width logic is per symbology.
- The character-class predicates and alphanumeric encoding values (`IsNumeric`, `IsAlphanumeric`, `GetAlphanumericValue`, `IsValidISO88591`) lived inside the Standard QR constants class, so the shared `TextAnalyzer` silently depended on the Standard QR table class until applying the namespace dependency rule exposed it. The predicates now live in the shared `CharacterSets`. The alphabets are identical across ISO/IEC 18004 and ISO/IEC 23941.
- A UTF-16 code unit compared as `Int16` is negative above U+7FFF. `TextAnalyzer`'s AVX2 and SSE2 tiers tested the ASCII (> 127) and ISO-8859-1 (> 255) thresholds with signed packed compares, so every char from U+8000 up counted as in range: surrogate halves (any emoji or other non-BMP char), U+FFFD and the CJK compatibility area. Auto-detection then declared Latin-1 for text ISO-8859-1 cannot represent, and the Byte-mode Latin-1 writer truncated it. The writer's own SSE2 tier saturates instead, so the corruption differed per architecture. The ARM64 tier was correct by construction, since its reduction, `UMAXV`, is unsigned.

  Threshold tests on char data must be unsigned, and at these two thresholds a bit test is both correct and cheaper than any compare (`c > 127` is "any bit from bit 7 up", `c > 255` is "any high-byte bit", one `vptest` on AVX2). A tier the dispatcher cannot reach on the test machine needs a parity test that calls it directly: AVX2 hides SSE2 on every CPU that has it, so the dispatch-level test cannot see a defect only SSE2 has. `TextAnalyzerX64ParityTest` calls both entry points itself, as the ARM64 test always has.

- The core was never dependency-free on netstandard. SkiaSharp hid it by bringing `Span<T>`, `ArrayPool<T>` and `Unsafe` in through its own dependency on `System.Memory` and `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe`. Removing SkiaSharp broke only the netstandard2.0 and 2.1 builds, with 170 errors, and nothing on net8.0+. The shims are now referenced explicitly at the versions SkiaSharp pins, so a consumer of both packages resolves one copy. "Zero dependencies" is a statement about net8.0 and net10.0 and means "BCL shims only" on netstandard, as every document using the phrase says.
- Removing a dependency is a `using` audit. The library had no `using SkiaSharp;` lines, because the root namespace `SkiaSharp.QrCode` resolved every `SK*` type implicitly, and neither had the tests (`SkiaSharp.QrCode.Tests`), the Playground (`SkiaSharp.QrCode.Playground`) or the Benchmark. Every namespace move turned the hidden imports into compile errors, when the core split moved the library into two projects (2026-09-04) and again when it renamed the Playground (2026-09-05), and IDE0005 then pointed at the usings that had become redundant.
- `CentralPackageTransitivePinningEnabled` rewrites nuspecs, promoting every pinned transitive package into a direct dependency of a packed project (for 1.x, the SkiaSharp native assets beside SkiaSharp). Turning it off changed nothing a consumer resolves, so the promotion was only a declaration, never a dependency. It is off repository-wide (see "Package graph").
- C# 14 extension blocks emit public nested marker types (`<G>$hash`, `<M>$hash`) that metadata readers and reflection both see, and they broke the documentation trimmer, the shipped-documentation test and the approved-API listing at once. The rule everywhere is to skip nested types with an unspeakable name. The members are listed on the enclosing class, which is what a caller writes.
- A guard needs a negative test. The nupkg dependency assertion passed on its first run and produced four errors given the shipped 1.1.1 package, the cheapest possible falsification, which every future artifact-level check should repeat.
- Two assemblies through one reflection tool means two PDBs and two XML files that overlap: PolySharp emits the same documented polyfills into both, so a naive dictionary merge throws on the first shared key. Exported types never collide, so keeping the first entry is correct.
- A seam needs its own contract tests, not the kernel's. The luminance tier-parity tests proved the tiers agree with each other, but nothing proved what the bytes mean until the BT.601 formula and the white compositing were written into a test. That test caught its own author's wrong assumption: all-zero bytes with an alpha channel are transparent, so white, not black. A hand-written converter makes the same error, which is why the `TryDecodeImage` documentation states the rule.
- "Writable against the public surface" has two readings: a third-party adapter can decode through `TryDecodeImage` and render through `GetModuleRectangles`, but cannot get the first-party fast path. The plan took the phrase in the second sense and published the luminance kernels, but the maintainer's rule is the first: the public surface grows on request, not in anticipation, because an API is added in a minor version and removed only in a major, so the kernels went back to internal. Building the rendering project with the `InternalsVisibleTo` grant removed gives the exact list of what it still uses. Reading the code produced a list one third that size.
- Product name, package ID and repository URL are three strings that used to be one. After the rename, `FeatherQR` is the product, `SkiaSharp.QrCode` survives only as the metapackage ID, and the repository URL changed last. The mechanical rewrite worked only with a lookbehind for the repository owner and a lookahead for dotted project names, and the README's header and installation blocks were written by hand.
- GitHub Pages project sites do not follow a repository rename, and shared Playground links carry their settings in the URL hash, which a meta refresh drops, so the user-site stub forwards by script and keeps the meta refresh only as the fallback when script does not run. `user.github.io/<name>/` resolves to the project site first and the user site's folder second, so the stub is invisible until the project site is gone, which is expected, not a deployment failure.
- Transitive pinning, a file-based tool and a rename each reached further than the plan expected. The plan's inventory, taken before the split (2026-09-04), expected one `InternalsVisibleTo` use and found three, expected zero core dependencies and found the netstandard shims, and expected the dependency assertion to be a literal table but had to decide the pinning question first. Each was caught by a check against the artifact rather than the source: the metadata test, the nupkg guard, and the compiler with the grant removed.

- A default NativeAOT publish on x64 is limited to SSE4.2 and GFNI, and the JIT can reproduce its dispatch without an AOT compile. Under ILCompiler 10.0.9, `Vector256`, `Avx2` and `Bmi2` report false on any CPU, while SSE2 through SSE4.2, POPCNT and GFNI are still detected, so SSE-family tiers keep running. `DOTNET_EnableAVX=0` makes the JIT report exactly the same flags, and `DOTNET_EnableHWIntrinsic=0` turns them all off. The instruction set is spelled `x86-64-v3`. `x86-x64-v3`, a spelling found in older documents, is rejected as unknown.
- A dispatch has to read `IsSupported` itself to compile as it does today. Moving every dispatch onto `bool` properties declared in one table kept ILC's code and the JIT's machine code for the kernels the same, but not the JIT's inlining: `ModulePlacer.MaskCode` stopped being inlined into its caller, and `TextAnalyzer.Analyze` inlined 167 methods instead of 9 before dropping its dead tiers. Of four forms (a property, an aggressively inlined property, a `static readonly` field and the direct read), the JIT inlined the dispatch into its caller only for the direct read. Under ILC, a dispatch comparing a tier enum keeps a compare per branch and every unreachable branch, while a `bool` property folds away like the direct read. So the table is checked against the dispatch, not read by it.
- A list of tiers worked out by reading the code was wrong where it mattered. The first inventory, made by reading the gates, put `EccBinaryEncoder` on SSSE3 under a default NativeAOT publish (it runs 128-bit GFNI there), and missed the three kernels with no tier for one architecture: the Structured Append parity and scanner have none for x64, and the rMQR value writers none for ARM64. All of it was in the code, but only the builds' own reports found it.
- A tier is named for the minimum it needs, and a kernel can require more: `EccBinaryDecoder` runs 256-bit GFNI on `Gfni.V256` alone, while `EccBinaryEncoder` also requires AVX2. `Gfni.V256` stays true under `DOTNET_EnableAVX2=0`, so the table keeps each kernel's own condition. Not every combination of the CPU-dependent instruction sets in a class is a real CPU either: with AVX present, a CPU with GFNI also has its 256-bit form, so in that class the two depend on the CPU as one group.
- On ARM64 the useful knob is `DOTNET_EnableArm64Dp=0`, which shows on an Apple M2 what a core without the dot-product instructions runs. `DOTNET_EnableArm64AdvSimd=0` turns everything off on .NET 8 and is ignored on .NET 10, and a NativeAOT binary ignores both. ILC checks for the dot-product instructions at run time instead of deciding from the target instruction set: `Dp.IsSupported` reports true under `IlcInstructionSet=armv8-a` on an M2, and on the linux-arm64, win-arm64 and osx-arm64 runners.
- Moving a loop out of its method changes the code around it, even when the loop compiles the same. Moving the Standard QR row-mask and bit-expansion loops into inlined methods in their family files kept every loop identical, instruction for instruction, under the JIT (.NET 8 and 10, with and without AVX) and ILC (x64, `x86-64-v3`, ARM64), but added 2 to 22 instructions per call around them: a larger frame, a spill, reloads, reordered blocks. Passing the index and the threshold vector in removed one of them. Nothing in C# controls register allocation or block layout, and a file layout is not worth different machine code, so tiers move between files only as whole methods, whose disassembly stayed identical in all seven configurations.
- This machine cannot measure a difference of a few instructions per call. ShortRun and 20-iteration rounds of the image decode and encode benchmarks, alternating before and after, put the same build 9 to 37 % apart from itself on half the rows, so a layout change must produce disassembly identical to the previous commit.
