- ILC can produce ARM64 code on an x64 machine with no ARM64 linker. The publish stops at its linker check before ILC runs, but ILC itself, run on the x64 response file retargeted to ARM64, compiles and writes its disassembly, which is all a codegen comparison needs.
- Interpreted and AOT-compiled WebAssembly run the same tiers. The Mono interpreter reports 128-bit vectors as accelerated, as the AOT build does, so a Blazor WebAssembly app that never turns AOT on runs the same vector tiers as the Playground, and one build class covers both.

- A change of a few percent needs the fastest of interleaved runs, not a benchmark job. When the decode refactors of 2026-09-29 were judged on this machine, the `ShortRun` job gave error bars as large as the mean on some shapes (Micro QR `M2_512px`, 5,613 ± 15,843 µs), three launches of fifteen iterations moved one tree 23 % between two runs (Standard QR version 40 at 3 px/module, 112.7 and 91.4 µs), and one process of a build could take 2.5 times as long as another on a 4 µs decode. A small harness over both trees, alternating eight to twelve times and keeping each shape's fastest round, first quartile and median, stayed within a percent. The benchmarks remain for absolute numbers.
- Even then a shape can lean with the shapes that share its process. rMQR's gradient image measured +0.4 to +1.4 % in six runs of the rMQR shapes alone, two of them with part of the change taken back out, and −1.0 to −1.4 % in both runs of every shape. A lean that survives taking out the code it is blamed on is not caused by that code.
- The order of an A/B run can fake a regression. Two rounds that ran the base first each time put rMQR's image decode 15 to 21 % behind after the candidate scan was shared and moved Micro QR's failing paths by 16 to 25 %, while three rounds with error bars and the order alternated put every shape within 1 to 4 % and inside its error bars (2026-10-01). A machine that drifts during a run favours whichever tree runs first.

- Portable vector code in a default NativeAOT publish is limited to SSE2: SSSE3 through SSE4.2 are run-time checks there, usable by explicit intrinsics behind `IsSupported` but not by portable operations. Per 4,096 vectors, a saturating `Vector128.ConvertToInt32` took 52 µs against 3 under `x86-64-v2`, and a variable `Vector128.Shuffle` 43 against 3. A tier's flags do not show how its operations are compiled. Only timing it on the build does.
- WebAssembly's runtimes disagree on a cast: the interpreter produces `int.MinValue` for NaN and for values past 2^31, while AOT-compiled code saturates. An AOT build still interprets some methods, so a scalar sampler's output outside the image depended on how it ran. Every tier clamps before it converts, passing the conversion only values it converts exactly.
- Mono's WebAssembly AOT compiles some portable operations as calls into corlib's software fallback. 64-bit lane shifts were one, and the mask tier ran 8x slower than scalar until they went through `PackedSimd`. A new WebAssembly kernel's AOT profile is checked for corlib calls.
- The interpreter charges per operation and per call, and hoists nothing: a constant a helper builds is rebuilt on every call, a vector step costs about as much as three modules in scalar code, and a call ends a jiterpreter trace, so a step that wins in a probe can lose inside its kernel. The interpreter's break-even point is higher than AOT-compiled code's (chunks of 80 chars against 32 for the Structured Append walks, and 44 stream bits per eight columns against 27 to 33 for rMQR's pair planes), and since one flag gates both WebAssembly builds, the threshold follows the interpreter. Each shape is timed in its own process: an unchanged kernel ran 1.8x slower after another build's shapes had run in the same process.
- On the interpreter, a fixed cost per decode hides behind a share. With jiterpreter traces off, a decode runs 4 to 8 times longer but pays the same µs, so the fixed cost's share shrinks. Compare µs instead. Stopwatch probes change what they time there (2.7 µs added to one tree's read, none to the other's), so they can rank causes, but only an A/B of unprobed builds settles the question. Splitting the image decode into shared steps (2026-09-29) costs a Micro QR M4 read 2 to 4 µs interpreted: the same methods run as often as before, plus five wrappers, and inlining every wrapper that could go without undoing the split won none of it back.
- A dispatch change reaches callers on builds whose cell did not change. A branch that folds away still stopped the JIT from inlining its method, because the JIT judges by the IL before folding. An operand that takes an argument's address (a span's `Length`) made the .NET 10 JIT copy the span under a flag that is constant false. ILC kept a flag property as a call until it was `AggressiveInlining`. A changed method was inlined into just one of its five callers, making that caller 86 to 139 instructions longer (`DecodeWithMirrorRetry`, `NoInlining` since). Compare the callers' listings too, with `DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0`, since tier-1 code follows the run's profile.
- ILC inlines less than the JIT: it kept two small helpers with `out` parameters as calls inside rMQR's format reader, where the JIT inlined them.
- An interpolated exception message is compiled into the method that throws it, on every build. The rMQR extraction dispatch's two messages made it several times the size of its working path. With them moved out, it went from 530 to 102 instructions on the ARM64 JIT.
- `--parity` through a dispatch only checks the tier the CI machine picks. Every ARM64 runner has the dot-product instructions, so ILC's ARM64 code for the 128-bit luminance tier never ran in CI until `--parity` called the tier directly.
- A share has to come from timing a stage alone. A per-function sample put the Structured Append walks at 2.4 % of a set and the segmenter at 13 to 18 %, but timed alone the planner was 17 to 49 %, because the scalar walks run inside the segmenter's functions. The span API's shapes never run the bit packer, which only the data-object API calls.
- Bound a step's gain by its share times its saving before building variants of it, and then measure the step end to end. For the rMQR writers on WebAssembly that bound was 2.5 %, known from the first kernel timing, and the step moved encodes by 0.97 to 1.02, inside the spread. For the Standard QR Alphanumeric writer on ARM64 it was the same 2.5 % at version 40: two runs of nine rounds read 0.95 to 0.96 and 0.98 to 1.00 of the encode's time, 0.98 together, and its stage rows gave 2.5 % both times, so it ships (2026-10-05). The bound ranks the candidates. It is not the bar.
- The JIT needs its warmup. Under the timing mode's default 300 ms, the JIT can still be tiering on a shape of a few µs (Micro QR and rMQR images at 16 to 26 µs, against 5 to 6 after 3 s, on the ARM64 .NET 8 JIT). A median far above the minimum means tiering, not the code.
- A clear of a few bytes is a call when its length is a variable, and a call a row can cost more than one clear of everything. With the core moved into its quiet-zone window in place and each gap between two rows then cleared by `Span.Clear` of its 2q bytes, the quiet zone took 1.30 to 1.44 times each symbology's old clear of the whole destination and copy of the rows, from M1 to version 6. With each gap cleared as the row after it moved, still by the call, it took 1.21 to 1.32. An 8-byte store through `BinaryPrimitives` ending where the gap ends, zeroing each gap as the row after it moved, took it to 0.95 to 1.04 there, 0.91 at version 19 and 0.73 at version 40, in two kernel runs at gaps of 4 and 8 bytes (2026-10-06). A `Span.Clear` of the constant length took 0.87 to 0.99 of the stores' time on the margins alone (2026-10-06). rMQR had cleared its margins with the variable-length calls since it wrote into the strided window, and its quiet zone cost it about as much as Micro QR's full clear did: 1.12 to 1.20 times the quiet-zone-free encode, against 1.23 to 1.26 (JIT with AVX2).
- Where a placer may write past a row decides when the margins can be cleared. Micro QR's vector unpack runs past a row's end, but only with the row's packed bits past the core, which are zero, so the placer can write the strided window after the margins are cleared and leave them light, and the clear of a gap can spill into the row before it. Stores that zero exactly the gap, which would let the margins be cleared after any placer, cost 3 to 5 ns more on M1 to M4. Writing the window directly, in place of clearing the whole destination and copying the rows of a core built in a stack buffer, took Micro QR's quiet zone from 1.23 to 1.26 times its quiet-zone-free encode to 1.06 to 1.09 on the JIT with AVX2, and to 1.03 to 1.11 on the other builds measured, the JIT without AVX2 in runs of Micro QR alone (2026-10-06). Without AVX2 in a process that also encoded the other symbologies, the code at the phase's commit read 1.10 to 1.21 in two runs (base 1.18 to 1.23), for a cause not found, and the code after its review 1.07 to 1.08 in the second.
- A helper called once a row is a call on the WebAssembly interpreter. The gap clear, moved into a method of its own for the three symbologies, cost nothing measurable on the JIT, which inlined it, or on WebAssembly AOT, but the interpreter called it once a row. In one run of the small symbols (Micro QR M2 to M4, three rMQR sizes and Standard QR versions 1 and 6), that call made the quiet-zone encodes take 1.04 to 1.19 times as long as with it inlined, and marked `AggressiveInlining` they read 0.96 to 1.03 of the old code (2026-10-06). A refactor that adds a call a row is measured on the interpreter, whatever the other builds show.
- A clear of a constant few bytes is a store only where the compiler expands it. .NET 10 writes a `Span.Clear` of 8 or 16 bytes as one store in any block. .NET 8 does so only in a block its profile saw run and leaves the other a call for as long as the process runs, so a process that encoded Micro QR at quiet zone 6 and then at 2 or 4 cleared each gap with a call: M2 took 171 to 177 ns, against 164 to 172 before the phase and 140 to 150 when the process had started at 2 and 4. Stores through `BinaryPrimitives`, which .NET 8 inlines in any block, write the gaps on the builds before .NET 10 (2026-10-06).
- A path that is even or faster on .NET 8 and later can be slower on .NET Framework 4.8. Moving Standard QR's core into its window in place took 1.13 to 1.26 times the clear and copy there to version 20 in one process of a kernel, with one or two stores a gap, and the vector packer's scalar loop, which folds any byte to 0 or 1, took 1.4 to 1.6 times the multiply-gather on a matrix of 0 and 1. So the netstandard2.0 build keeps the clear and copy. Standard QR's pack takes the gather wherever the packer has no vector step (2026-10-06).
- A netstandard build is judged on the runtimes that load it, not on its sibling's. netstandard2.1 kept Standard QR's clear and copy untimed, on .NET Framework 4.8's reading of netstandard2.0. On .NET 6 and 7, which load it, the move cost no symbol more end to end at quiet zones 4 and 6 (its quiet zone 0.3 to 2.1 % of a version 1 to 40 encode, against 0.5 to 2.6 %), and its kernel took 0.71 to 0.99 of the clear and copy with one store a gap, as on .NET 8, so netstandard2.1 moves the core (2026-10-07).

- An output default is judged by the readers people carry. Every library reader agreed with the Kanji output, and the standard supported Kanji mode for a segment with no ECI, yet an Android phone's own scanners read none of it, so the default went back to UTF-8 and Kanji mode became an option. The phone scan came after the default had changed. It belonged before.
- An option has to reach every path that analyses the text, not only the paths the tests take by default. When `AllowKanji` was threaded through the three generators, a mutation pass turned each call site's argument to `true` and to `false`, and found three paths no test took with the option set: the refusal's advice, version resolution under a range or the boost, and Micro QR's ranged sizing.
- A byte-for-byte comparison through the public API catches what the tests do not. Run against the previous commit on every entry point, sizing call and refusal, it found that a Micro QR refusal message had changed for every text, not only Kanji text: the edit had dropped a space. No test checked the other texts' wording.
- A hand edit to a generated file has to go into the generator. The committed forward Kanji table's comments had been reflowed by hand, but the template had not, so regenerating the table rewrote 31 lines with no data change. The template was brought in line, and regeneration now reproduces the committed file byte for byte.
